prompt: In the exposed-bucket incidents the lesson lists, what did the people who found the data need?
hint: The bucket answered as designed.

choices.text: Stolen credentials of an employee
choices.why: No credentials at all: the buckets answered anonymous requests.

choices.text: Only the bucket's address
choices.why: Right. Nothing was broken into; the setting did what it said.

choices.text: Access to the provider's data centre network
choices.why: The provider's security held throughout.

choices.text: A vulnerability in S3 that AWS later patched
choices.why: S3 worked as designed in every case; nothing was patched.

prompt: Three of the four 2017 incidents in the table share a shape. Which one?
hint: Whose bucket, and whose data?

choices.text: A bucket made public by an attacker who had broken in first
choices.why: The owners made them public; nobody broke in.

choices.text: Data deleted by ransomware after it was found
choices.why: The table records exposure, not deletion.

choices.text: A vendor's bucket holding a customer's data
choices.why: Right. The company in the headline never created the bucket, and its programme never saw it.

choices.text: A bucket encrypted with a key that was later leaked
choices.why: Encryption at rest does not stop a request the bucket is configured to answer; lesson 11 says why.

prompt: Put AWS's changes in the order it announced them.
hint: The guardrail came first, the defaults years later.
items: every new object encrypted at rest by default
new buckets created with Block Public Access on and ACLs disabled
trap: The defaults of 2023 are not the guardrail itself, which dates from 2018.

prompt: Since April 2023 new buckets start with Block Public Access on. Which bucket of a clinic's account does that change protect least?
hint: A default applies when something is created.

choices.text: A bucket whose objects are encrypted with SSE-S3
choices.why: Encryption says nothing about who may read; and the date is what matters here.

choices.text: A bucket created in 2021 and never changed since
choices.why: Right. Buckets created before the change keep the settings they had.

choices.text: A bucket created this morning by caio
choices.why: That one got the new defaults.

choices.text: A bucket created this year with a bucket policy granting the clinic's own users read access
choices.why: A grant to the account's own users is not public, and the guardrail is on anyway.

prompt: The letter was public with no bucket policy at all. Which grant made it so?
hint: It was set at upload, on the file.

choices.text: The bucket's default encryption, which was off
choices.why: Encryption decides nothing about who may read.

choices.text: A grant to `AllUsers` in the bucket's ACL, which every object inherits
choices.why: A bucket ACL's READ lets people list keys; objects do not inherit it.

choices.text: The fact that moto accepts any key
choices.why: The request had no key at all; the object's ACL answered it.

choices.text: A grant to `AllUsers` in the object's ACL
choices.why: Right: `--acl public-read` on `put-object`.

prompt: Everybody holds `READ` on the clinic's referrals bucket through its bucket ACL. What does that let a stranger do?
hint: READ on a bucket is not READ on its objects.

choices.text: Read every letter in the bucket
choices.why: Objects have their own ACLs; a bucket ACL's READ does not reach their contents.

choices.text: Delete the bucket
choices.why: READ grants no deletion.

choices.text: List every key, which here is a list of patients' cases
choices.why: Right. File names alone can be personal data.

choices.text: Change the bucket's policy
choices.why: That needs a different permission entirely.

prompt: bia's report carries a grant to `AuthenticatedUsers`, and an anonymous `curl` gets `403`. Who can read it on AWS?
hint: The group is not the users of your account.

choices.text: Only principals in the same region
choices.why: Regions play no part in the grant.

choices.text: Only the clinic's own IAM users
choices.why: That is the belief that makes this grant dangerous.

choices.text: Nobody, since the anonymous request was refused
choices.why: The refusal is only for unsigned requests; a signed one from any account is answered.

choices.text: Anybody who signs the request with a key from their own AWS account
choices.why: Right, by AWS's documentation; the lab cannot show a stranger's key.

prompt: Why did the lesson not show an anonymous listing of the bucket with `curl`?
hint: A transcript has to prove something.

choices.text: moto answers it for any bucket, private or not, so it would prove nothing
choices.why: Right. The grant itself is what the review looks for.

choices.text: Listing a bucket anonymously is illegal
choices.why: It was your own bucket in your own lab; the reason is moto's behaviour.

choices.text: `curl` cannot send the request a listing needs
choices.why: A listing is a plain GET on the bucket.

choices.text: The bucket was empty
choices.why: It held the letter.

prompt: Match each grant to who it answers.
hint: The figure's right-hand column.

pairs.right: everyone, for every object it names
everyone, as a list of keys

prompt: The ACL group that means everybody on the internet, signed in or not, is called `___`.
hint: The other group is AuthenticatedUsers.

prompt: Match each Block Public Access switch to what it does on AWS.
hint: Two are about new grants, two about existing ones.

pairs.right: refuses a request that would add a public ACL
makes public ACLs already written grant nothing
refuses a bucket policy granting public access
limits a public-policy bucket to AWS services and its own account

right_distractors: encrypts every object with a managed key

prompt: A bucket has an object ACL granting `AllUsers` READ. Somebody switches on `BlockPublicAcls` alone. On AWS, is the object still public?
hint: One switch is about new grants, another about old ones.

choices.text: No, the switch removes the grant
choices.why: No switch removes anything; they refuse or ignore.

choices.text: Yes, until `IgnorePublicAcls` is on too
choices.why: Right. `BlockPublicAcls` refuses new grants; only `IgnorePublicAcls` makes the existing one count for nothing. That is why all four go on.

choices.text: No, any one switch makes the whole bucket private
choices.why: Each switch closes one door; the existing ACL is a different door.

choices.text: It depends on whether the object was uploaded before the switch
choices.why: Upload time does not matter; which switches are on does.

prompt: With all four switches on, moto still served the letter and accepted a new public ACL. What does that tell you?
hint: Lesson 1's table.

choices.text: That the ACL was written before the switches, so they do not cover it
choices.why: `IgnorePublicAcls` exists for exactly the grants written before.

choices.text: That Block Public Access does not work on AWS either
choices.why: AWS documents both refusals; moto simply does not enforce them.

choices.text: That moto stores the guardrail and enforces none of it
choices.why: Right. On AWS the anonymous request is refused and the `put-object-acl` gets `AccessDenied`.

choices.text: That the switches take some minutes to apply
choices.why: Nothing waits; moto never applies them.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the account-level switches the ones worth having?
hint: Think of the bucket somebody creates next year.

choices.text: They are cheaper, since bucket-level switches are billed
choices.why: Neither level is billed.

choices.text: They replace bucket policies entirely
choices.why: They sit above policies; they do not replace them.

choices.text: They also cover buckets nobody has created yet, and a bucket's own setting cannot loosen them
choices.why: Right. The bucket level protects one bucket; the account level protects the ones you do not know about.

choices.text: They are the only ones moto enforces
choices.why: moto enforces neither level, and the account level could not even be reached in the lab.

prompt: What does Object Ownership set to `BucketOwnerEnforced` do, by AWS's documentation?
hint: It closes three of the four routes at once.

choices.text: Encrypts every object with the bucket owner's key
choices.why: It is about ownership and ACLs, not encryption.

choices.text: Disables ACLs: no ACL is consulted, and access comes from policies alone
choices.why: Right, and it is the default for new buckets since April 2023.

choices.text: Refuses any bucket policy that names another account
choices.why: Policies are untouched; that would be a different control.

choices.text: Makes the owner's account the only one that can list the bucket, whatever the ACL says, and nothing more
choices.why: It goes further: no ACL is consulted at all, for listing or for reading objects.

prompt: `clinic-reports` did not answer the checker's anonymous request. Which line caught it?
hint: A probe without a signature cannot see the grant that needs one.

choices.text: `ANSWERS AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST`
choices.why: That line appeared only for the referral letter.

choices.text: The ACL line about every AWS account reading it
choices.why: Right. Reading the lists is what catches the grant that refuses the anonymous test.

choices.text: A policy line, since the bucket had a public policy
choices.why: It had no policy at all.

choices.text: None; the checker missed it
choices.why: It printed the ACL line and the missing guardrail.

prompt: How many findings did the first run of `public_buckets.py` print for `clinic-referrals`?
hint: The lines indented under its name.

prompt: Why does the checker report a policy statement that has a condition, instead of deciding the condition makes it safe?
hint: What can a program not know about the clinic?

choices.text: Because any condition at all makes a statement public
choices.why: A condition can only narrow; the question is by how much.

choices.text: Because boto3 cannot read conditions
choices.why: boto3 returns the whole policy; the choice not to judge is deliberate.

choices.text: Because whether it narrows the grant enough is a reading for a person
choices.why: Right. Same rule as lesson 8: the checker finds where something is open, a person decides.

choices.text: Because conditions are ignored by AWS as well as moto
choices.why: AWS applies conditions; only moto ignores them.

prompt: Which of these does `public_buckets.py` check for every bucket? Choose all that apply.
hint: Its parts, in order.

choices.text: Whether Block Public Access is fully on
choices.why: Right, the first check.

choices.text: Whether the bucket policy allows something to everyone
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether objects are encrypted
choices.why: Not in this program; encryption is lesson 11.

choices.text: Whether each object answers a request with no credentials
choices.why: Right, the probe, on your own buckets only.

choices.text: Who last changed each bucket's policy
choices.why: That needs the record of API calls, lesson 15.

prompt: In what order does the lesson fix an exposed bucket?
hint: The last step is the only one that tells you the others worked.

choices.text: Encrypt the objects, then rotate the keys
choices.why: Encryption does not change who the bucket answers.

choices.text: Put the guardrail on, ask again, then remove the grant
choices.why: Asking before removing the grant proves nothing about the fix; and AWS refuses `BucketOwnerEnforced` while the bucket ACL grants others.

choices.text: Remove the grant, put the guardrail on, ask again as the stranger
choices.why: Right: take it away, stop it coming back, then prove it.

choices.text: Delete the bucket, create a new one, copy the files back
choices.why: Somebody needed the sharing; without a better way the grant returns elsewhere.

prompt: The clinic's website must be readable by everybody. Which arrangement does the lesson describe, by AWS's documentation?
hint: Even this bucket can stay private.

choices.text: A private bucket read by a CloudFront distribution through an origin access control
choices.why: Right. The public reaches CloudFront; nobody reaches the bucket directly.

choices.text: A bucket ACL granting `AuthenticatedUsers` READ
choices.why: That lists the keys to any AWS account and serves no visitor without one.

choices.text: Presigned URLs for every page
choices.why: Presigned URLs expire, and are for one recipient at a time.

choices.text: A public bucket with a policy allowing `GetObject` to everyone, and Block Public Access off for it
choices.why: That works and is exactly the exception the account-level guardrail would have to carry.

prompt: In the lab, what carried the final `403` for the letter?
hint: Which half of the fix does moto apply?

choices.text: `BucketOwnerEnforced`
choices.why: Stored by moto, not enforced.

choices.text: The object's public grant being removed
choices.why: Right. On AWS the guardrail would also hold if the grant came back.

choices.text: The checker running
choices.why: The checker only asks; it changes nothing.

choices.text: Block Public Access on the referrals bucket
choices.why: moto enforces none of it; the letter was served with it on.

prompt: The setting that disables ACLs on a bucket is Object Ownership set to `___`.
hint: Bucket owner, enforced.

prompt: A new account policy says: Block Public Access on at the account level, and every bucket `BucketOwnerEnforced`. Which of the four routes can still make an object readable by a stranger on AWS? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three routes are ACLs, and the fourth is the one BlockPublicPolicy refuses.

choices.text: A bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"`
choices.why: `BlockPublicPolicy` refuses it at the account level.

choices.text: A grant to `AuthenticatedUsers`
choices.why: It is an ACL, and ACLs are off.

choices.text: None of them, by AWS's documentation
choices.why: Right. ACLs are not consulted, and a public policy is refused.

choices.text: An object ACL granting `AllUsers` READ
choices.why: With ACLs disabled, no ACL is consulted.
